source: Sim, Eiger, Kohno (2026) AI-Enabled Human Memory Manipulation: Misleading AI-Generated Summaries Distort Human Memory
finding: Loftus-style misinformation effect with an AI source. People who read an AI-written summary with a wrong detail later recalled the original event worse.
numbers: Online study N=328 (four cells of 80 to 83). Traffic-sign question correct: 83.6% after a consistent summary vs 44.8% after a misleading summary, chi2=53.9, p<.001. Human-labelled vs AI-labelled summary made no difference (chi2 1.18 consistent, 0.14 misleading, n.s.).
limits: One video paradigm, 24-hour delay, forced two-way recognition only; Prolific sample. The LLM is the misinformation source, not the subject.
agent_relevance: A wrong line in a summary or memory note can override the original evidence when it is re-read. Keep the raw source next to any summary.

source: Sim, Eiger, Kohno (2026) AI-Enabled Human Memory Manipulation: Misleading AI-Generated Summaries Distort Human Memory
finding: Audit of LLM video summaries: errors are frequent, and omission of the central event is the most common.
numbers: ChatGPT and Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite, 20 summaries of 2 classic videos. Central details omitted 51.6% on average; 95% of summaries omitted the collision; 7 to 21 errors per summary (average 305 words); 65% had inaccurate central details; 60% had at least one hallucinated addition, about 1.6 per summary.
limits: Two short videos only; fast model tiers; not a systematic sample.
agent_relevance: Compression into prose is lossy in specific ways (omission, addition, order). A summary should never be the only record.

source: Sim, Eiger, Kohno (2026) AI-Enabled Human Memory Manipulation: Misleading AI-Generated Summaries Distort Human Memory
finding: The misinformation effect held for both video versions.
numbers: Stop-sign video chi2=37.995 (phi=-.481); yield-sign video chi2=25.002 (phi=-.390); both p<.001. Power plan: at least 63 per cell for 80% power at a medium effect.
limits: Forced choice (stop or yield) can make a wrong-detail effect look larger than in free recall.
agent_relevance: Plausible wrong details need a check against source, not a re-read.

source: Xu et al. (2026) When Agents Misremember Collectively: Exploring the Mandela Effect in LLM-based Multi-Agent Systems (ICLR 2026)
finding: Social-contagion false memory in LLM agent groups. MANBENCH tests whether agents adopt a false shared memory from peers across 4 task types and 5 interaction protocols.
numbers: 4,838 multiple-choice questions, 20 tasks. Baseline error: GPT-5 17.63%, Llama3.1-8B 44.58%. Under social influence all models rose; GPT-5 more than doubled to 41.59% (role-based short-term). Qwen-235B rose from 25.48% to 74.75% (role-based short-term).
limits: Multiple choice with simulated peers; the false memory is injected context, not self-generated.
agent_relevance: Samples that quote each other can lock in a falsehood. Matches guardrail G4: agreement among samples is not proof.

source: Xu et al. (2026) When Agents Misremember Collectively: Exploring the Mandela Effect in LLM-based Multi-Agent Systems (ICLR 2026)
finding: Short-term (in-context) false memory is much stronger than long-term, and models differ.
numbers: GPT-5 reality-shift rate fell from 31.03% (role-based short-term) to 1.67% (role-based long-term). Claude 3.5 Haiku and Qwen3 stayed high (63.67% to 55.63% for one). Claude 4 Sonnet shift 15.45% generic vs 35.21% role-based short-term; GPT-4o 46.04% vs 55.95%.
limits: Depends on model family, not only size.
agent_relevance: In-context contamination is the danger. A durable store read fresh may help for some models only.

source: Xu et al. (2026) When Agents Misremember Collectively: Exploring the Mandela Effect in LLM-based Multi-Agent Systems (ICLR 2026)
finding: Group size first raises then lowers the effect; model size does not protect.
numbers: Role-based groups: effect peaks, then with 9 or more agents error falls below the baseline (under 32%). Maximum reality shift rose from 89.3% (8B) to 92.2% (235B), an inverse scaling trend. General Knowledge: baseline error 9.40% but shift 48.06% in the generic short-term protocol.
limits: The authors explain the drop at 9 or more agents as suspicion; this was not tested.
agent_relevance: More voters is not safe by default; scale does not remove the bias.

source: Xu et al. (2026) When Agents Misremember Collectively: Exploring the Mandela Effect in LLM-based Multi-Agent Systems (ICLR 2026)
finding: Prompt defences cut the effect: cognitive anchoring (state own prior knowledge, test group claims against it) and source scrutiny (check where a claim came from).
numbers: Reality-shift rate cut from 46.0% to 17.8% by cognitive anchoring and to 26.5% by source scrutiny in the short-term setting. Abstract: average 74.40% reduction with prompt plus alignment-based defences.
limits: Authors' benchmark; defences tried on the same tasks. Anchoring helps most in short-term settings.
agent_relevance: A cheap scaffold step: write own answer before reading peers or memory, then compare.

source: Li and Li (2026) What Should an Agent Forget? Separating What Is Stored from What Is Used (RD-Forget)
finding: An LLM agent method that suppresses superseded memories at read time while keeping them stored. It is the closest engineering analogue to retrieval-induced forgetting. Suppression links are same-slot only, and history becomes eligible again when the question asks about the past.
numbers: Five suites, four backbones. Dropping forgetting lowers matched-Full scores: 91.86 to 68.60 (AMB-Text), 93.59 to 60.26 (LME-KU), 74.00 to 51.00 (MAB-FC); deficits 23.26, 33.33, 23.00 points. Dropping query conditioning costs 13.95, 11.54, 18.00 points. Fact consolidation gain over best baseline 11 to 26 points.
limits: Suppression is explicit and set by a frozen LLM curator, not emergent as in human RIF. Results are by the authors.
agent_relevance: Shows the useful side of forgetting. Suppress by slot and by question intent, never by blanket decay. Scope the suppression so siblings survive.

source: Li and Li (2026) What Should an Agent Forget? Separating What Is Stored from What Is Used (RD-Forget)
finding: Scope matters: recency alone cannot tell a competing value from a complementary relation, so suppression must respect the facts on the reasoning chain.
numbers: BEAM Qwen 50.21% vs 32.84% (ACE) and 34.75% (ReasoningBank); PersonaMem Qwen 59.93% vs 39.21% and 38.17%. Best in all 12 model-benchmark combinations of the main comparison and 8 of 8 in the second table.
limits: Baselines are other memory frameworks, not plain long context.
agent_relevance: A sibling-protecting rule: suppress only items that fill the same slot as the new item.

source: Chao et al. (2026) STALE: Can LLM Agents Know When Their Memories Are No Longer Valid?
finding: Leading-premise errors on models. Models can say a belief is outdated but still answer from the old state when the question presupposes it.
numbers: 400 scenarios, 1,200 queries. Gemini-3.1-pro Type I: State Resolution 92.0% but Premise Resistance 30.0%. Qwen3.5-27B 76.0% to 4.0%. Best overall 55.2%; GPT-5.4 22.4%; GPT-4o-mini 9.8%.
limits: Authors' benchmark; LLM judge agreed 95.8% with humans.
agent_relevance: Leading questions work on models too (Loftus-type). Test a question's premise against current state before answering.

source: Chao et al. (2026) STALE: Can LLM Agents Know When Their Memories Are No Longer Valid?
finding: Old and new facts coexist in memory with no adjudication: the old one is retrieved alongside the new one.
numbers: In LightMem, new evidence appears in retrieval for 77.5% of state and premise cases and 67.8% of policy cases. At write, the top-3 recalled entries hold the old evidence in 60.5% of cases, yet only 3.3% of these are judged to need an update. Without a stale premise the top-1 old rate is 25.5%, yet failure stays 78.6%.
limits: One memory framework analysed in depth.
agent_relevance: Retrieving a sibling does not suppress it. A check step should explicitly retire the old fact.

source: Chao et al. (2026) STALE: Can LLM Agents Know When Their Memories Are No Longer Valid?
finding: Specialised memory systems did not fix it. A write-time adjudication step helped.
numbers: Memory frameworks overall between 5.1% and 17.8% (A-mem 8.3, mem0 17.8). CUPMEM (KEEP, STALE, REPLACE, UNKNOWN labels at write time) 68.0% overall; Premise Resistance 78.0% (Type I) and 75.0% (Type II); about $0.37 per instance.
limits: Prototype by the benchmark authors with a predefined state schema.
agent_relevance: Supports an active vs stale label in our memory, in line with guardrail G2.

source: Kwon (2026) Reclaim Evaluation: A Lossy Memory Is Worse Than an Empty One
finding: A compressed memory that keeps the wrong conclusion but drops the source makes the model re-emit the error with confidence; an empty memory leads it to abstain.
numbers: Fixed-budget compression test. Reclaim rate after correction: lossy 0.00 at the wall, source-first up to 1.0 on the arithmetic example. A one-prompt distiller reclaims 0.49 to 0.88 with a weak writer and 1.00 with a frontier writer. On a deployed-agent benchmark lossy RR is about 0.14 at every scale (3B to frontier) vs 0.60 to 1.00 for source-first.
limits: Single independent author; synthetic drift tasks; strongest where the source is compact.
agent_relevance: When the agent compresses a lesson, keep the recomputable source and drop the stale conclusion. A memory can carry an error like a false-memory trace.

source: Kwon (2026) Reclaim Evaluation: A Lossy Memory Is Worse Than an Empty One
finding: Capability does not remove the wall, and a length-matched filler control shows the fix is content, not extra text.
numbers: 8B and frontier models fail at the same place. Benefit of capability is an inverted U: gap +0.46 at partial source, 0.00 at both ends. Under a mandatory tool interface open models commit the wrong action 0.78 to 0.96 of the time; one frontier model refuses; in an agentic task models refire 0.77 to 0.91 with no abstention.
limits: Some regimes marked only suggestive by the author.
agent_relevance: Do not expect a better model to repair a bad memory format.

source: Deng and Sinchaisri (2026) Stale, Misattributed, or Late: Where Personal Memory Fails Before Generation
finding: Memory errors made before generation: stale values and wrong-person facts. Serving only the active slot value removes stale exposure.
numbers: Without update resolution 70.3% of prompts expose a superseded value (benchmark revises 80% of chains). Keyed memory: 92.9% of 7B completions hold the current value vs 70.4% keyless (difference 0.225, CI 0.161 to 0.296). Merge recall on LongMemEval never above 0.062. A 5% false-merge rate loses the current value on 6.1% of queries; 20% gives 22.5% and clean retrieval 0.553.
limits: Controlled synthetic revision data; two small frozen models.
agent_relevance: Over-suppression has a cost: false merges silently delete the current value, the sibling-loss side of RIF. Measure both stale exposure and lost-current rate.

source: Deng and Sinchaisri (2026) Stale, Misattributed, or Late: Where Personal Memory Fails Before Generation
finding: Misattribution (a source-monitoring error) survives validity filtering.
numbers: An entity posterior cut wrong-person exposure from 0.121 but could not separate identically named speakers in LoCoMo. Frozen models reproduce prompt errors in generated text.
limits: Dataset specific.
agent_relevance: Memory items need a source tag, or a lesson may be applied to the wrong case.

source: Barman et al. (2026) The Geometry of Forgetting
finding: Embedding retrieval spaces reproduce human forgetting and false memory with no tuning. Forgetting comes from competition among neighbours, not from time.
numbers: Power-law forgetting exponent b=0.460 +/- 0.183 (human about 0.5) with competitors vs about 0.009 without. Production embeddings put variance in about 16 effective dimensions. DRM critical-lure false alarm 0.583 vs human 0.55 over all 24 DRM lists, 5 seeds, threshold 0.82 giving zero unrelated false alarms.
limits: Sentence-level encoder on isolated words; authors say other encoders are untested. Tests interference forgetting, not retrieval-induced forgetting.
agent_relevance: Our vector memory will produce DRM-style false recall of plausible absent siblings. Source attribution or verification is the mitigation the authors name.

source: Chattaraj and Raj (2026) LLMs Remember First, Forget Last: Dual-Process Interference in Large Language Models
finding: Classic interference paradigms on 39 LLMs (1B to 2.5T parameters). Proactive interference hurts far more than retroactive, the reverse of the usual human result.
numbers: Effect size d=1.73. Retroactive accuracy 93.9% at N=3 updates, 96.0% at 50, 72.9% at 100, 45.5% at 200, 24.6% at 300. Proactive accuracy falls from 94% to 3%. Hallucination under 1%.
limits: Their RI means retroactive interference, not retrieval-induced forgetting. One in-context value-tracking task, temperature 0.
agent_relevance: Models favour first-seen values, so an old lesson can intrude over a new one. Tag items by recency.

source: Chattaraj and Raj (2026) LLMs Remember First, Forget Last: Dual-Process Interference in Large Language Models
finding: Scale and reasoning help retroactive resistance only. The authors note the proactive intrusion pattern resembles retrieval-induced forgetting.
numbers: Parameter count explains 49% of variance in retroactive score (R2=0.491) and 6% in proactive (R2=0.06, n.s.); context window R2=0.003. The two scores correlate r=0.21 (CI -0.11 to 0.49). Reasoning models 178.0 vs 150.3 (18.4% higher). o1 first on retroactive (186.4) yet 35th on proactive (22.0). Intrusions skew early: 14% return the very first value at N=3.
limits: The RIF resemblance is a remark by the authors, not a test.
agent_relevance: Reasoning models do not protect against old-value intrusion. Test recency separately.

source: Yousuf et al. (2025) Can an LLM Induce a Graph? Investigating Memory Drift and Context Length
finding: Forgetting and intrusion in long context on relational recovery: drift starts earlier than needle-in-haystack tests suggest, through lost edges and invented ones.
numbers: Memory drift rises sharply after about 2,000 tokens for GPT-4o and Gemini-2; o1 drifts more than GPT-4o beyond 2,000 tokens.
limits: Graph reconstruction, not a memory-psychology paradigm; weak link to RIF.
agent_relevance: Keep working sets small for relational work.

source: Cai (2026) Benchmarking Factual Robustness of LLMs via Multi-conversation Persuasion
finding: Models stay consistent with their own earlier output (refusal inertia), which hides how persuadable they are once history is wiped.
numbers: SAST-IR design: stateful attacker, stateless target. Per-model numbers were not extracted this session.
limits: Mechanism only.
agent_relevance: Own earlier output in context acts as a consistency anchor: good against attack, bad when the earlier answer was wrong. A fresh-context check removes it.

source: Loprinzi, Shopeju, Storm (2026) Temporal effects of exercise on retrieval-induced forgetting
finding: Large replication of a claim that exercise preserves RIF over time failed. Classic RIF replicated, but its size shrank from first to second test in all groups.
numbers: N=372, five groups of 71 to 77. Rp- recall below Nrp- (RIF present). RIF smaller at the second test across groups, driven by better recall of suppressed items. No exercise benefit.
limits: Category-exemplar task; young adults.
agent_relevance: Human suppression is temporary and recoverable on re-test. Do not rely on lasting suppression.

source: Raaijmakers and Jakab (2011) Retrieval-induced forgetting without competition
finding: RIF appeared even when practice recalled the category name, with no competition between items, against the inhibition account.
numbers: Two experiments; RIF found in both without competitive retrieval during practice.
limits: Favours interference or blocking accounts over inhibition; the debate is open.
agent_relevance: Strengthening one item can harm siblings even with no direct competition, so no lesson-writing step is neutral.

source: Loftus and Palmer (1974) Reconstruction of automobile destruction
finding: Founding misinformation study: the verb in a question changed speed estimates and later report of broken glass.
numbers: From memory, not opened: smashed 40.8 mph vs hit 34.0 mph; a week later 32% vs 14% reported broken glass (none present).
limits: Figures recalled from background knowledge; verify before citing.
agent_relevance: The model for the leading-question tests that STALE and Sim et al. repeat on LLMs.

source: Anderson, Bjork, Bjork (1994) Remembering can cause forgetting
finding: Founding RIF study: retrieval practice of some category members lowers later recall of unpracticed members of the same categories.
numbers: Not opened; no figures given here (exact numbers belong to angle A documents).
limits: Rivals: inhibition vs interference or blocking (see Raaijmakers and Jakab line).
agent_relevance: The paradigm behind the warning that one lesson may suppress siblings.

source: Murayama, Miyatsu, Buchli, Storm (2014) Forgetting as a consequence of retrieval: a meta-analytic review
finding: Meta-analysis of the RIF literature supporting a reliable effect.
numbers: Not opened; effect size not stated here.
limits: Exact numbers belong to angle A documents.
agent_relevance: Human baseline for sizing any LLM RIF test.
